keycloak-37429.issue: Wrong locale script: The new `totpStep1` text is written in Traditional Chinese (您的手機、應用程式) while this is the `zh_CN` (Simplified Chinese) message bundle. All surrounding keys in this file (e.g. `totpStep2`, `totpStep3`, `configureAuthenticators`) use Simplified Chinese, so users of the zh_CN locale will see a mixed-script message. The text should be rewritten in Simplified Chinese (e.g. 在您的手机上安装以下应用程序之一：).

Wrong language: The new `totpStep1` value is in Italian ("Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:") while this is the Lithuanian (`messages_lt.properties`) message bundle. Lithuanian users will see Italian text on the account page. The previous Lithuanian text was replaced rather than translated; the same mistake also appears in the login `messages_lt.properties` file in this PR. The value should be translated to Lithuanian (e.g., "Įdiekite vieną iš šių programų savo mobiliajame telefone:").

Dangling reference: The new `totpStep1` text says "Installera en av följande applikationer på din mobil:" ("Install one of the following applications on your mobile:"), but no list of applications follows anywhere in this message or the diff. The previous text named FreeOTP and Google Authenticator explicitly; the replacement now points to a list that does not exist in this file, so users see an instruction referencing an empty/missing list unless some other (unchanged) component renders the app list separately. Worth confirming that the list is actually supplied elsewhere before merging.

Possible rendering bug: The message now uses ICU `ChoiceFormat` syntax (`{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}`). This only renders correctly if the consumer formats the message with Java `MessageFormat`. The account UI is a React/JS application; if its message formatting (e.g., a JS-based substitution of `{0}`-style placeholders) does not implement `ChoiceFormat`, the raw `{2,choice,...}` expression will be shown to end users whenever the multivalued attribute error is displayed. Worth verifying that the account-ui frontend actually supports choice-format messages before merging; the same change was also applied to the admin-ui messages file, so a shared formatter may cover it, but that is not evident from this file.

Wrong Language: The Lithuanian translation of `loginTotpStep1` was replaced with Italian text ("Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:"). Lithuanian users will see an Italian instruction on the login page. The original Lithuanian sentence (with the FreeOTP/Google Authenticator links) should be translated to Lithuanian instead of copied from the Italian locale, consistent with the other locales in this PR which received properly translated text.

sentry-95633.issue: Shared pool shutdown bug: The `FixedQueuePool` is created once in the factory's `__init__` and shared by every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` returned from `create_with_partitions` (arroyo calls this per partition assignment, and strategies can be recreated on rebalance). However, `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which stops and joins all worker threads in the shared pool. Closing or joining one partition's strategy therefore kills the workers used by every other live strategy, silently halting message processing for the rest of the consumer. The pool's lifecycle should be owned by the factory (which already shuts it down in `shutdown()`), not by each strategy.

max_workers semantics: In `thread-queue-parallel` mode, `max_workers` is repurposed as the number of queues (`num_queues=max_workers or 20`). Besides the changed meaning (the CLI help now says "maximum amount of parallelism", which is arguably consistent), a falsy `max_workers` value such as `0` silently falls back to 20 queues instead of raising a validation error, unlike other modes where worker counts are passed through explicitly. Low severity, but worth validating or documenting.

Data loss on processing failure: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, the `finally` block calls `complete_offset` even when `result_processor` raised an exception. The exception is only logged, so the offset becomes committable and the commit loop will advance past a message whose processing failed, silently dropping it. For an at-least-once consumer this converts a transient error (e.g., DB timeout) into permanent data loss. Either the offset should remain outstanding on failure (for retry) or the failure should be surfaced to the framework.

Shutdown drops queued items: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before calling `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`. The worker loop condition `while not self.shutdown` causes each worker to exit after finishing its current item, without draining items still sitting in its queue — even though `immediate=False` is meant to allow pending items to be consumed. On graceful shutdown, any backlog in the queues is discarded (offsets for those items were already added, so they will be committed as done once prior offsets complete... actually they stay outstanding, but the work is lost and the strategy's "no item is lost" guarantee is broken during close).

Unbounded memory for stalled partitions: `OffsetTracker.all_offsets` is only pruned in `mark_committed`. If a partition's commit is permanently blocked by one stuck offset (e.g., a group whose queue is backed up), `all_offsets` and `outstanding` grow without bound for that partition, and `get_committable_offsets` scans `range(start, max_offset + 1)` over the full span every second in the commit loop, degrading over time. Consider pruning completed offsets below the contiguous watermark instead of only at commit time.

Flaky assertion: In `test_stats_reporting`, the assertion `stats["total_items"] > 0` is made immediately after submitting 10 work items, but worker threads may have already consumed and processed some or all of them by the time `get_stats()` is called (the pool has no pause mechanism). On a fast machine or under load reordering, `total_items` can be 0 and the test fails intermittently. The subsequent `total_items == 0` check after the completion event is safe, but this first check should be removed or made race-tolerant.

Overly strict assertion: `test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 hashed group keys land on exactly 3 distinct queues (`len(queue_indices) == 3`). This relies on `hash()` distribution; while it will almost always pass with 20 samples, it is a probabilistic assertion with no guarantee, making the test theoretically flaky. Asserting `queue_indices <= set(range(3))` (valid indices) would test the actual contract without the distribution assumption.

Test contradicts implementation: In `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling`, the mocked processor raises for the first message, but the worker's `finally` block in `OrderedQueueWorker.run` calls `complete_offset` regardless of whether processing succeeded. That means both offsets become committable and the strategy's commit loop (which fires every ~1s) will commit past the failed message. The test's final assertion (`len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`) therefore depends on a race: if the commit loop runs within the ~2.2s polling window, the test fails. Either the production code should not complete offsets on failure, or the test should assert the actual (commit-anyway) behavior; as written it is flaky and encodes contradictory expectations.

Resource leak on failure: In the new `test_thread_queue_parallel*` tests, `factory.shutdown()` is called after the `with mock.patch...` block rather than in a `finally`/fixture. If any assertion inside the block fails (these tests are timing-based and inherently flaky), `shutdown()` is never reached and the pool's daemon worker threads and commit thread keep running for the rest of the test session, potentially polluting other tests that patch the same processor class.

Private API usage: The Kafka integration test drives the arroyo `StreamProcessor` via `processor._run_once()` and `processor._shutdown()`, which are private methods and can break silently on arroyo upgrades. It also monkeypatches `factory.create_with_partitions` on the instance with a `# type: ignore[method-assign]`. Consider using the public `run()`/`signal_shutdown()` API or a short-lived thread instead.

calcom-22532.issue: Possible Bug: The call `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` passes an empty `data` object. Prisma's `updateMany` with an empty data object performs no update (and in some Prisma versions raises a validation error for empty data), so the stated intent — refreshing `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` — is not achieved. The schema changes in this PR add `updatedAt` to the `CalendarCache` model, not to `SelectedCalendar`, so it's unclear this field even exists on `SelectedCalendar`. If the goal is to bump a timestamp, the data argument must specify the field (e.g., `data: { updatedAt: new Date() }`), and the schema must define it.

Performance: This write runs unconditionally on every availability fetch/refresh cycle, issuing an `UPDATE` across all selected calendars for the credential even when nothing was fetched (the call is outside the `if` that guards `fetchAvailability`). For users with many calendars this adds a needless write per sync tick; consider only bumping the timestamp when a fetch actually occurred, or relying on the `CalendarCache.updatedAt` added in this PR, which already tracks cache freshness per credential.

Unconditional extra DB query: The handler now always instantiates `CalendarCacheRepository` and calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` on every `connectedCalendars` request, adding a `groupBy` query to a frequently-called endpoint even when the caller has no Google calendars or the calendar-cache feature is disabled (the mock returns `[]`, but the real repository shown performs the query unconditionally). If the repository does not internally gate on the feature flag, this adds latency to every calendar fetch for all users. Worth verifying whether the query should be skipped when the cache feature is off or when `credentialIds` is empty.

Portability Bug: `sed -i '' -E ...` is macOS/BSD syntax only. On Linux, `sed -i ''` treats `''` as the input file name and the actual env file as the backup suffix, so the in-place update of `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` fails (or corrupts files) on Linux machines. Since this is a dev/test helper script likely run on varied machines, use a portable form (e.g., detect OS or use `sed -i.bak`).

Fragile Path: `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is resolved relative to the current working directory, not the script's location. Running the script from any directory other than `scripts/` will silently create a new `.env` in the wrong place (the `touch` fallback masks the mistake) and update the wrong file, leaving the real `.env` pointing at a stale webhook URL.

Stale URL Reuse: When Tunnelmole is already running, the URL is scraped from `/tmp/tmole.log`, which may be from a previous session with a different tunnel URL (tunnels can change between runs, and the log is only cleared when this script starts tmole itself). The script then writes that stale URL into `.env` as `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL`, so Google webhooks would target a dead endpoint with no error surfaced.

Minor UI nit: The wrapping `<div className="flex w-32 justify-end">` is now rendered unconditionally around `CredentialActionsDropdown`, but that component returns `null` when the connection is a delegation credential without cache (or modification is disabled). Previously the whole actions block was omitted in that case; now an empty 8rem-wide flex container is rendered inside `AppListCard`'s actions slot, which can shift layout/spacing on cards with no visible actions. Consider rendering the wrapper div conditionally or moving it inside the dropdown component.

Hardcoded locale: The cache timestamp is formatted with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)`, which ignores the user's locale even though the component uses `useLocale()` for translations. Users with other locales will see dates formatted in US style (e.g., MM/DD/YYYY) while all surrounding text is localized. Use the locale from `useLocale()` (or `Intl.DateTimeFormat(undefined, ...)`).

Stale cache status: After `deleteCacheMutation` succeeds, the component only calls `onSuccess?.()` and does not invalidate the `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` query (unlike `disconnectMutation`, which invalidates it in `onSettled`). If a parent does not pass an `onSuccess` callback that refetches, the dropdown will keep showing "Last updated" cache status for a credential whose cache was just deleted, until an unrelated refetch happens.

grafana-80329.issue: Increased cleanup frequency: The cleanup ticker interval is reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This makes the cleanup job run 10x more frequently, increasing database load (especially since the annotation cleanup now runs repeated batched queries/deletes per cycle). If the intent was only to make cleanup more responsive for the annotation deadlock fix, a hardcoded 1-minute interval for all cleanup tasks may be too aggressive; consider making the interval configurable or confirming the load impact is acceptable.

Error-level logging: Routine cleanup progress is logged with `r.log.Error` (e.g. "Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time", "Tags to clean", and the count-based/tag equivalents). These are informational messages on the happy path, not errors, so every cleanup cycle will emit error-level log entries and trigger alerting/noise in deployments that page on ERROR logs. They should be `Debug`/`Info`. Additionally, logging the full `ids` slice can dump thousands of IDs per batch into the log at error severity.

Possible infinite loop: `untilDoneOrCancelled` terminates a batch only when `affected == 0`. In the MaxCount path, the batch condition uses `LimitOffset(batchSize, cfg.MaxCount)`; if a delete affects rows but the same SELECT keeps returning deletable rows with affected > 0 this is fine, but if `deleteByIDs` returns 0 affected while `fetchIDs` returned IDs (e.g., rows deleted concurrently between SELECT and DELETE, or a dialect reporting 0 affected rows), the loop stops prematurely even though work may remain — conversely, on databases where RowsAffected is unreliable the loop could spin. Worth verifying termination semantics against the drivers in use; the old single-statement loop had the same shape but re-ran one idempotent statement, whereas this version can diverge between what SELECT sees and what DELETE reports.

sentry-80168.issue: Incomplete abstract handler: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now inherits from `StatefulDetectorHandler` but provides no implementation. `StatefulDetectorHandler` defines abstract members such as `build_occurrence_and_event_data` (newly added as `@abc.abstractmethod` in this PR) and requires `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, and `get_group_key_values` from subclasses. If any of these are decorated with `@abc.abstractmethod`, instantiating `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` will raise `TypeError`; if not, calling `evaluate` on it will fail at runtime (e.g., missing `counter_names` or unimplemented `build_occurrence_and_event_data`). Since the class previously returned an empty list as a placeholder, the new inheritance silently changes it from a harmless no-op to a broken handler. Either implement the required methods or keep it as a placeholder until the metric-alert detector is actually built.

Silent duplicate handling: The old code explicitly logged an error ("Duplicate detector state group keys found") and skipped duplicate group keys. The new dict-based `results[result.group_key] = result` silently overwrites earlier results with no logging, so a duplicate group key now silently drops occurrences/state for the first result. If duplicates are still considered "shouldn't happen", the error logging/investigation signal is lost; if they're now acceptable, the last-wins semantics should be documented.

Possible enum conversion bug: `PriorityLevel(new_status)` constructs a `sentry.types.group.PriorityLevel` from a `DetectorPriorityLevel` value. This only works if the two enums' values are numerically identical for every non-OK status; otherwise it raises `ValueError` (or maps to an unintended priority) at evaluation time, failing the whole detector evaluation. If the enums are guaranteed to share values, an explicit mapping or comment would make that contract clear; otherwise this needs a safe conversion.

Test data mismatch: In `test_state_results_multi_group`, the second occurrence is built with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(detector.detector_handler, "group_2", 6, ...)` but the data packet contains `group_2: 10`. The value 6 is wrong; the test currently passes only because the mock builder happens not to incorporate the value into the occurrence, but it misrepresents the scenario and will silently mask regressions if the builder ever starts using the value.

sentry-80528.issue: Dead code / config bug: In `get_monitor_environment_context`, a copy of `monitor.config` is made and `schedule_type` is converted to its human-readable display value, but the returned dict uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the original, unconverted config), so the conversion is silently discarded. The context sent with the occurrence will contain the raw `schedule_type` integer instead of the display string. This code was moved verbatim from `mark_failed.py`, so the behavior is unchanged, but since the file is new it is worth fixing here: either use the mutated `config` copy or drop the copy/conversion lines.

Docstring typos: The `get_failure_reason` docstring contains typos ("humam readible") and its third example ("A failed check-in was detected") does not match any actual output, since the singular branch always uses a specific status like "An error check-in was detected". Minor, but misleading for future readers.

grafana-76186.issue: Context discarded: `TestLogger.FromContext` ignores both the receiver's existing context and the passed `context.Context`, returning a brand-new `NewTestLogger()`. Per the `Logger` interface contract ("returns a new contextual Logger that has this logger's context plus the given context"), it should carry over the receiver's accumulated context. In practice this means any test asserting that log calls made via a context-derived logger include the original logger's context will silently pass or fail incorrectly, since the returned logger shares no state with the original. Low severity since it only affects test fakes, but the fake no longer models the real `grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext` behavior it is meant to stand in for.

Possible Bug: The fallback path in `FromContext` silently discards the request context when the type assertion to `*log.ConcreteLogger` fails: it returns `d.New()`, a logger with only the wrapper's original context, dropping any contextual attributes stored in the incoming `ctx` (e.g., the pluginId/endpoint/dsName added by the new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware`). If `infra/log.Logger.FromContext` can return a non-`*ConcreteLogger` value (e.g., a different wrapper or value type), log lines produced via this path would silently lose all request-scoped fields with no error or log indicating the fallback occurred. Consider logging a warning on the fallback branch, or verifying that the assertion can only fail in cases where dropping the context is acceptable. Note: the behavior of `infra/log.Logger.FromContext` was not shown, so whether the assertion can realistically fail is uncertain; the impact if it does is loss of contextual log fields.

Breaking interface change: Adding the required `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` method to the `Logger` interface is a breaking change for any out-of-tree implementations of this exported interface (e.g., external plugins or libraries wrapping the plugin logger). Any such implementation will fail to compile until it adds the new method. In-repo implementations (`fake.go`, `logger.go`) are updated in this PR, but external consumers are not. If this package is intended as a public plugin API, consider whether a default/adapter helper or a separate optional interface would be preferable.

Lost traceID logging: The PR removes the `traceID` field from the "Plugin Request Completed" log line (previously obtained via `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)`). The new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` added elsewhere in this PR enriches the context with `endpoint`, `pluginId`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, and `uname`, but not the trace ID, so this information is dropped entirely from plugin request completion logs. This makes it harder to correlate plugin requests with distributed traces when debugging. If intentional, it should be noted; otherwise the trace ID should be added to the contextual attributes or retained here.

grafana-103633.issue: Cache key collision: `userPermDenialCacheKey` concatenates `userUID`, `action`, `name`, and `parent` with underscore separators and no escaping. Since these are user-controlled resource identifiers (e.g., a dashboard name or folder UID containing underscores), two distinct tuples can produce the same key — e.g., action `dashboards:read` with name `a_b`/parent `c` collides with name `a`/parent `b_c` for the same user. A collision would cause a cached denial for one resource to incorrectly deny access to a different resource. Note the existing `userPermCacheKey` shares this pattern, but the new function widens the collision surface by adding two more unbounded components. Using a delimiter that cannot appear in these values (or hashing the components) would avoid this.

Behavior change: caching disabled: The in-process authz client previously went through `newRBACClient`, which wrapped the gRPC client with `cache.NewLocalCache` (30s expiry). It is now constructed with `&NoopCache{}`, which disables client-side caching entirely for the local (non-Zanzana) path. If this is intentional (e.g., because the authz `Service` now does its own permission/denial caching, making a second cache layer redundant), it would help to note that in the PR description or a comment; otherwise this silently removes a 30-second cache and increases gRPC round-trips for every check.

Misleading test name: The subtest "Fallback to the database on outdated cache" does not actually exercise an outdated cache entry. The cache is populated with permissions for `dashboards:uid:dash1` only, while the check is for `dash2`, so this is a plain cache miss (identical to the previous subtest except for the extra cache write). A genuinely outdated cache would contain a stale entry for the requested resource (e.g., `dashboards:uid:dash2: false`) and assert the service still falls back to the database — a scenario worth covering since the new `Check` path returns the cached result whenever `checkPermission` says allowed, and only falls back when it does not. As written, the test name overstates what is verified.

Stale denial cache: The new `permDenialCache` is only ever written (on deny) and read; there is no code path that deletes an entry when a user's permissions are granted. Since the denial check runs first and short-circuits before `permCache` is consulted (the new test even asserts the permission cache "is not checked"), a user who is later granted access to a resource will keep receiving `Allowed: false` until the short TTL expires, even after `permCache` has been refreshed with the new permission. If permission changes elsewhere invalidate `permCache` immediately, the denial cache introduces a longer effective staleness window for deny results than for allow results. Consider deleting the denial key (or keying denials off the same invalidation signal as `permCache`) when a check succeeds via cached or fresh permissions.

Silent error swallow: In `Check`, errors from `getCachedIdentityPermissions` are ignored wholesale (`if err == nil`). This is fine for `cache.ErrNotFound`, but the function can also return real errors (e.g., from `GetUserIdentifiers` or `fmt.Errorf("unsupported identity type: ...")`). Those are silently swallowed and the request falls through to the DB path, which will likely hit the same error again — doubling the work and skipping any distinction between a cache miss and a genuine failure. Consider only falling through on `cache.ErrNotFound` and handling other errors explicitly.

grafana-79265.issue: Type Inference Bug: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` is declared without a type annotation, so TypeScript infers the property's type as `undefined`. The interface in `packages/grafana-data/src/types/config.ts` declares it as `number | undefined`, but any code that later assigns a number to `config.anonymousDeviceLimit` (e.g., from the frontend settings payload) will fail to compile against this class. It should be declared as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;` (or initialized to `0` to match the backend default).

Weak test assertion: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that the second `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. It does not verify that the existing device ("32mdo31deeqwes") was left intact, nor that a subsequent update of an *existing* device still succeeds when the limit is reached (the intended behavior of the `updateDevice` fallback path). As written, the test would pass even if the store rejected all writes once the limit was hit, which would break legitimate returning anonymous devices. Consider adding a case where the same existing device is updated and asserting `NoError`, plus a `ListDevices` check on final state.

Performance regression: TagDevice was previously invoked asynchronously in a goroutine with its own timeout, so anonymous authentication was never blocked on the device-store write. It is now called synchronously on the request path using the request's context, meaning every anonymous request pays the latency of a DB count + insert/update (and under device-limit contention, an extra CountDevices query). Under DB slowness or lock contention this directly adds latency to all anonymous traffic, and a slow store can now stall request handling. Consider keeping the call async, or at least bounding it with a timeout as before.

Lost panic recovery: The removed goroutine had a recover() that converted a panic in TagDevice into a warning. TagDevice is now called inline, so any panic inside the device service (e.g., during DB access) propagates into the authentication middleware and can turn an anonymous request into a 500 instead of degrading gracefully. If TagDevice is guaranteed panic-free this is moot, but the previous code deliberately guarded against it.

Behavior change: `TagDevice` now returns the error from `tagDeviceUI` instead of logging it and returning nil. This changes the contract for all callers of `TagDevice`, not just the anonymous client path: any caller that previously treated tagging failures as non-fatal will now receive errors (including transient DB failures), and tagging aborts entirely on the first failure. In `client.go` non-limit errors are only logged so authentication continues, but if `TagDevice` is invoked from other paths not shown here, they may start surfacing errors where none were returned before. Verify all call sites tolerate the new error propagation.

DI regression: `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` now constructs the store inline via `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore(sqlStore, cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit)` instead of receiving an `anonstore.AnonStore` through dependency injection. This hard-wires the DB store implementation, making it impossible to inject a fake store for this service in tests or alternative builds, and silently discards whatever store the caller previously provided. If this was done to centralize limit configuration, consider keeping the injected interface and configuring the limit inside the store provider instead.

Race condition: The device-limit check in `CreateOrUpdateDevice` is a non-atomic count-then-act: it calls `CountDevices`, compares against `deviceLimit`, and then inserts. Two concurrent anonymous requests can both observe `count < deviceLimit` and both insert, exceeding the limit. Under load (which is exactly when the limit matters) the cap will be overshot. Consider enforcing the limit atomically in SQL (e.g., conditional insert or a transaction with a lock).

Misleading error: `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` whenever `rowsAffected == 0`, but that also occurs when the device exists yet its `updated_at` falls outside the 30-day window (e.g., a known device that has been idle for more than 30 days, or whose stored `updated_at` is slightly in the future beyond the 1-minute slack). In that case the device is never refreshed and the caller is told the limit was reached, conflating two distinct situations and permanently freezing stale devices once the limit is hit. A separate signal (or an upsert that refreshes stale rows) would distinguish "device unknown/expired" from "limit reached".

Inconsistent windows: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` counts devices using a window anchored at `time.Now()`, while `updateDevice` updates using a window anchored at `device.UpdatedAt`. If the request's `UpdatedAt` differs from the current time (clock skew, replayed timestamps, or a client-supplied value), the two checks use different ranges, so a device may be counted as active but then fail the update-window predicate (or vice versa), producing inconsistent limit enforcement.

calcom-22345.issue: Brittle SQL assertions: The updated assertions compare `Prisma.Sql` fragments for deep equality against hand-written SQL strings (e.g. `Prisma.sql`("userId" = ${...}) AND ("teamId" IS NULL)``). `Prisma.Sql` equality depends on exact string segments and parameter values, so any innocuous whitespace or formatting change in the service's query construction will break these tests even when the generated SQL is semantically identical. Consider asserting on the semantic result (rows returned by a query using the conditions) instead of exact SQL text, as the final `getBaseConditions` test already does.

Possible Bug: The constructor's `options` parameter type was widened to `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions`, where `teamId` is optional, but `buildTeamAuthorizationCondition` still expects `Extract<InsightsBookingServiceOptions, { scope: "team" }>` (which requires `teamId`). A caller can now construct the service with `scope: "team"` and no `teamId`; after the scope narrowing, `options.teamId` is `undefined` and is passed into `Prisma.sql`("teamId" = ${options.teamId}")...` and to `teamRepo.findByIdAndParentId({ id: options.teamId, ... })`, producing a query with `NULL`/undefined instead of a valid team id. Either the public type should require `teamId` for the team scope, or the code should guard against a missing `teamId` and return `NOTHING_CONDITION`.

Behavior change: `findMany` was removed and replaced by `getBaseConditions`, which returns raw `Prisma.Sql` instead of executing a query. Any caller that previously relied on `findMany` to run the query (with `select`, `take`, `orderBy`, etc.) must now compose its own `$queryRaw` with these conditions. If any call site was not migrated in this PR, it will break at compile time or, worse, silently lose the authorization scoping if it was rewritten to query without the conditions. Worth verifying all call sites were updated.

calcom-10967.issue: Inverted condition: The original code spread `{ slug }` into the organization create payload when `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` was false (`...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })`). The rewrite now spreads `{ slug }` only when `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` is true, inverting the behavior. When team billing is enabled, `slug` will no longer be set on the created organization (and `requestedSlug` in metadata will be set where it previously was not), which can break slug assignment/lookup for billing-enabled deployments. If the intent was only a stylistic cleanup, the condition should remain negated: `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`.

Inverted condition: Same inversion for `requestedSlug`: previously it was included in `metadata` only when `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` was true, and the new ternary preserves that — but note the two conditions now agree with each other whereas before they were complementary. Verify which behavior is intended: if `slug` on the organization and `requestedSlug` in metadata were deliberately complementary (slug set only when billing is disabled, requestedSlug only when enabled), the new code silently changes the billing-disabled path by dropping `slug` from the created organization.

Behavior change: In `createEvent`, the calendar filter now compares each candidate calendar's `externalId` only against the first (main host's) destination calendar. For a collective event where multiple hosts have destination calendars with different `externalId` values, calendars belonging to the other hosts will no longer match the filter and the event will not be created on them. If the intent is "create only on the main host's calendar" this is fine, but it is a real behavior change from the previous single-`destinationCalendar` semantics and deserves an explicit test covering the multi-host collective case.

Ignores credentialId: The Calendar interface in `packages/types/Calendar.d.ts` was changed to `createEvent(event, credentialId)`, and the Google service now selects the destination calendar by matching `cal.credentialId === credentialId`. This service ignores the `credentialId` argument entirely and always uses the first element of `destinationCalendar` (`mainHostDestinationCalendar`). In a collective event where multiple members have Lark calendars, the first entry may belong to a different credential than the one invoking `createEvent`, causing the event to be created on the wrong member's calendar (or a 404 from Lark). Consider matching on `credentialId` like the Google service does.

Possible Bug: In `updateEvent`, the fallback lookup `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` is only reached when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, but it then compares each calendar's `externalId` against that same falsy `externalCalendarId` (e.g. `undefined`). No calendar can match, so `selectedCalendar` is always `undefined` in this path, and `calendar.events.update` is called with an undefined `calendarId`, which will fail against the Google API. Previously the code fell back to `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. The intended logic was likely to find the calendar matching the event's destination (e.g. by credential or the first/main host entry), not by `externalCalendarId`.

Possible Bug: Same problem in `deleteEvent`: `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` is evaluated only when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, and comparing `cal.externalId === undefined` never matches, so `calendarId` becomes `undefined` instead of the previous fallback `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. Deleting an event without an explicit `externalCalendarId` will target an invalid calendar id.

Duplicate deletions for recurring bookings: The reference lookup changed from `find` (single reference) to `filter` + iteration over all calendar references. In the recurring-event branch inside the loop, the code still deletes events for ALL bookings (`updatedBookings`) using ALL of the user's calendar credentials, regardless of which `reference` is being iterated. For a recurring booking with multiple calendar references (e.g., collective events), this loop now runs once per reference, calling `deleteEvent` repeatedly for the same events and pushing duplicate entries into `apiDeletes`. Previously it ran only once. Consider hoisting the recurring branch out of the per-reference loop or deduplicating.

Possible Bug: In the recurring branch, `updBooking.references.find((ref) => ref.type.includes("_calendar"))` still picks only the FIRST calendar reference of each booking, so for collective bookings with multiple calendar references only one attendee's event is deleted per booking. Since this PR's purpose is to handle multiple hosts/destination calendars, this inner lookup likely should also be a `filter` and delete each reference's event; otherwise the multi-host fix is incomplete for recurring bookings.

Swallowed exception: The new try/catch in `loadUsers` converts any unexpected error (e.g., a Prisma connection failure or a bug in the mapping code) into a generic `HttpError({ statusCode: 500, message: "Unable to load users" })` without logging the original error anywhere. The caller and operators get no way to diagnose why user loading failed, since the root cause (stack trace, Prisma error details) is discarded. Add a `log.error` (or similar) with the original error before rethrowing the generic 500.

Team calendars not persisted: For COLLECTIVE team events, member `destinationCalendar`s are collected into `teamDestinationCalendars` and pushed onto `evt.destinationCalendar`, but the booking creation only connects `evt.destinationCalendar[0]` (the organizer/event-type calendar) via Prisma `connect`. The team members' destination calendars are used for the in-memory event but never linked to the booking record, so any later flow that reads `booking.destinationCalendar` (e.g., reschedule, cancel, payment webhooks) will not see them. If persisting all calendars is intended, `connect` should accept all collected ids; if not, the push into `evt` is misleading.

Nondeterministic order: `teamDestinationCalendars.push(...)` happens inside the async `users.slice(1).map(...)` callbacks, so the order of the pushed calendars depends on promise resolution order rather than the `users` array order. Downstream consumers that index into `destinationCalendar` (e.g., the `[0]` "main host" selection used by calendar services) can get a different member's calendar run to run. Collect the calendars synchronously (or map to the calendar and await afterwards) to keep ordering deterministic.

Possible Bug: `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is obtained by destructuring `evt.destinationCalendar ?? []`, so when `destinationCalendar` is null or an empty array (which other changed call sites now explicitly produce, e.g. `destinationCalendar: []`), it is `undefined` and `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` throws a TypeError. The old code used optional chaining (`evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`) and was safe in this case. The check should be `mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration !== "google_calendar"` (or explicitly handle the empty case).

Possible Bug: In `createAllCalendarEvents`, when a credential is not found in `this.calendarCredentials`, it is fetched from the DB, but only assigned if `credentialFromDB.app?.slug` is truthy. If the credential exists but has no associated app (or the DB fetch fails), `credential` remains `undefined` and `createEvent(credential, event, destination.externalId)` is still called with `undefined`, which will throw inside the calendar service instead of being skipped or reported. The `if (credential)` guard is outside this path only for the in-memory lookup, not after the DB fallback.

Possible Bug: In `updateAllCalendarEvents`, the same DB-fallback pattern leaves `credential` as `undefined` when the lookup fails (no app slug / not found), yet `result.push(updateEvent(credential, event, bookingRefUid, calenderExternalId))` is executed unconditionally afterwards, passing `undefined` as the credential to `updateEvent`.

Behavior change: `credentialId` for non-calendar (dedicated integration) results changed from `result.credentialId` to `undefined` in the first mapping block. Previously the booking reference stored the credential id returned by the non-calendar integration; now it is always dropped, which can break consumers that rely on `credentialId` in booking references for dedicated integrations. If intentional, it should be verified against the booking-reference schema/consumers.

Possible Bug: `externalCalendarId: isCalendarType ? result.externalId : undefined` (and the non-dedicated branch `externalCalendarId: result.externalId`) now dereferences `result` directly. `createEvent` in CalendarManager can return `undefined` (e.g. its 404 catch path returns `undefined`), in which case `result.externalId` throws a TypeError during booking creation, whereas the old code read from `evt.destinationCalendar` and did not depend on `result` being defined.

calcom-10600.issue: Accessibility regression: Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the password visibility toggle button removes it from keyboard tab order entirely. Keyboard-only users can no longer toggle password visibility, which is an accessibility regression (the button is still clickable and visible, so it should remain focusable). If the intent was to skip it during tabbing in some specific flow, a more targeted approach (e.g., only disabling tab focus while the field is autofocused, or using `aria-hidden` semantics appropriately) would avoid locking out keyboard users in all cases.

Confusing component name: The default-exported component is internally named `TwoFactor` while the existing `TwoFactor.tsx` component (TOTP input) also exports a component with that name. This makes imports and stack traces ambiguous between the TOTP code input and the backup code input; renaming the function to `BackupCode` would avoid confusion.

Backup codes overwritten on re-setup: Every call to the setup endpoint unconditionally regenerates and overwrites `backupCodes` in the database, even if the user never completes enabling 2FA (the endpoint also sets `twoFactorEnabled: false`). If a user starts setup, receives backup codes, abandons the flow, and later starts setup again (or the endpoint is invoked again for any reason), all previously issued backup codes are silently invalidated. A user who saved the first set of codes will find they no longer work at login. Consider only generating backup codes when none exist, or invalidating old codes only when 2FA is actually enabled.

Codes returned before verification: Backup codes are generated, persisted, and returned to the client during setup, before the user has confirmed the TOTP secret (verification happens in the enable endpoint). Combined with the unconditional overwrite, a client can repeatedly call this endpoint to rotate codes without ever enabling 2FA. Low severity on its own, but it amplifies the invalidation issue above and means codes exist for accounts where 2FA was never actually activated.

Unhandled exceptions: The backup-code path can throw an unhandled error and return a raw 500 instead of a meaningful error response. `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` will throw if the stored `backupCodes` value is corrupt or fails to decrypt (e.g., encryption key rotated), and `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll(...)` will throw a TypeError if the client sends a non-string value (e.g., an object or array in the JSON body). Both cases are attacker-controllable inputs to an auth endpoint and should be caught and returned as 400/500 JSON errors like the rest of the handler.

Code not consumed: Unlike the login flow (next-auth-options.ts), which marks a verified backup code as used and re-encrypts the remaining codes, this handler verifies the backup code but never consumes it. The comment says codes are deleted at the end, which is true only when the disable succeeds; if the request fails after verification (e.g., the session/user update throws), the code remains valid. Low severity since the only action gated here is disabling 2FA, but the inconsistency with the login path is worth noting.

Ineffective assertion: The PR adds a FIXME comment acknowledging that `expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` passes even when the switch is not checked, yet leaves the broken assertion in place. Since this test is the setup path that enables 2FA before backup-code tests run, a regression that silently fails to enable 2FA would not be caught here, and subsequent backup-code steps could fail with confusing errors (or worse, pass against a user without 2FA enabled). The sibling test below already shows the correct pattern (`data-state="checked"` visibility check) - applying it here would fix the issue.

Weak verification: The new backup-code dialog checks only that a success toast appears after clicking copy, and leaves the download file content and clipboard content as TODOs. As written, the copy test would pass even if the clipboard contains wrong or empty data, and the download test only verifies a filename, not that the codes were written. Given this feature handles account-recovery secrets, asserting the actual content (e.g., reading the download stream and checking it matches the displayed codes) would make these tests meaningfully verify behavior rather than UI clicks.

Unguarded JSON.parse: The decrypted `backupCodes` value is passed directly to `JSON.parse` with no try/catch. If the stored value is corrupted, was written by an older version, or decryption produces garbage (e.g., after a `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` rotation), `JSON.parse` throws a raw SyntaxError instead of a controlled `ErrorCode`. In the NextAuth `authorize` callback this surfaces as an opaque login failure with no useful error message for the user, and unlike the other failure paths (IncorrectBackupCode, MissingBackupCodes) it cannot be mapped to a friendly message by the login page. Wrapping the decrypt/parse in try/catch and throwing `ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes` or InternalServerError would keep the failure path consistent.

No format validation: The user-supplied backup code is matched with a plain `indexOf` against the stored list with no length/format check, even though the UI (BackupCode.tsx) enforces a 10-character format. Any arbitrary string is compared against every stored code. This is mostly a robustness nit, but note the comparison is not constant-time; for a low-value, rate-limited credential this is low severity, though a length check would also avoid pointless decryption-side work on junk input.

Possible Bug: After a successful TOTP enable, the flow now stops at `SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes` and only calls `onEnable()` from the "close" button. If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (ESC key, clicking the backdrop, or the dialog's built-in close affordance via `onOpenChange`), neither `onEnable()` nor `resetState()` runs. The parent component is never notified that 2FA was enabled (so its state/refresh is stale), and the modal's internal state (step, password, backup codes, blob URL) is not reset, so reopening the modal can land in a stale state.

Resource Leak: The object URL created via `URL.createObjectURL(textBlob)` is only revoked when a new setup run replaces it. If the user closes the modal (or unmounts the component) after generating codes, the blob URL is never revoked and the backup codes remain in component state (`backupCodes`, `backupCodesUrl`) — sensitive one-time credentials lingering in memory and a leaked blob reference. Consider revoking in a cleanup effect and clearing `backupCodes` in `resetState()`.

Type Safety: `useState([])` infers `never[]`, so `setBackupCodes(body.backupCodes)` (where `body` is untyped JSON from `response.json()`) relies on `any` to compile, and `backupCodes.map((code) => ...)` treats each code as `never`. Typing the state as `useState<string[]>([])` would make the contract with the API response explicit and catch malformed payloads at compile time rather than rendering `undefined.slice(...)` at runtime if the server response shape changes.

calcom-8087.issue: Fire-and-forget async: Making the `forEach` callback `async` means the returned promises are not awaited or collected. The `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` (and `deleteMeeting`) calls now run unawaited: `Reschedule` can complete before the deletions finish, and any rejection from `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` becomes an unhandled promise rejection with no way for the caller to learn about it. If a calendar API call fails, the event silently remains on the external calendar. Other call sites in this PR (e.g. `handleCancelBooking.ts`) were converted to a `for...of` loop with `await` for exactly this reason; this file should do the same (or use `Promise.all` over a `map`).

Unawaited async forEach: The `forEach` callback is now `async`, so the promises returned by `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` and `deleteMeeting(...)` are not awaited and are not collected. Consequences: (1) the surrounding `try` block can no longer catch errors from these operations — a failed calendar event deletion or meeting deletion is silently swallowed as an unhandled promise rejection; (2) `Reschedule` resolves before any of the deletions complete, so callers (e.g., the booking cancellation flow) may observe stale state or race with subsequent work. A `for...of` loop with `await` (as done in `handleCancelBooking.ts` in this same PR) or `Promise.all` over mapped promises would preserve error handling and completion semantics.

Unawaited async forEach: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` makes the callback async, but `forEach` does not await the returned promises. The surrounding router procedure will complete (and respond to the client) before the calendar `deleteEvent` calls finish, so failures are silently lost and any code after this block that assumes deletions are done will run too early. Unlike the sibling change in `handleCancelBooking.ts` (which was converted to a `for...of` loop with `await`), this call site keeps the fire-and-forget pattern. Since the callback has no try/catch and the promises are discarded, a rejected `deleteEvent` becomes an unhandled rejection. Use a `for...of` loop with `await` (or `Promise.all` over a map) instead.

Unawaited async forEach: The `.forEach(async (credential) => {...})` callback now awaits `getCalendar(credential)`, but `forEach` does not wait for async callbacks. The enclosing code continues (and the handler can finish/return) before the per-credential calendar deletions complete, and any rejection inside the callback becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Previously this was safe because `getCalendar` was synchronous; making the callback async silently changed the control flow. This block should be converted to a `for...of` loop with `await` (as done in the refactored block below it), or collected into `Promise.all`.

Error handling change: `await appStore[appName]` now awaits a dynamic `import()` promise. If a video app module fails to load (e.g., a broken build chunk or missing dependency at runtime), the dynamic import rejects and the error propagates out of `getVideoAdapters`. Previously, a plain object lookup could never throw, so callers like `deleteMeeting` and `getBusyVideoTimes` silently got an empty adapter list. Now a single failed module load can turn previously-tolerated flows into unhandled rejections (e.g., `deleteMeeting` has no try/catch around the lookup). Consider wrapping the await or catching import failures per-app so one broken app doesn't break all video operations.

Sequential loading: `getVideoAdapters` awaits each app module one at a time inside the loop. With multiple credentials of different app types, module loads are serialized rather than kicked off in parallel (e.g., via `Promise.all` over the lookups). This is a minor latency regression on cold starts, not a correctness bug.
